claims.text: The initial sub-10 nm equiatomic Au-Co-Cu-Ni-Pt nanoparticles are disordered solid solutions.
Below 15 nm, surface-energy minimization suppresses the kinetically sluggish-diffusion effect.
Surface-energy minimization drives rapid Ostwald ripening in these nanoparticles.
The smallest particles are lost through surface-diffusion-mediated transport of material to larger particles.
Surface-diffusion-mediated coarsening accelerates significantly above 600 K because the surface-diffusion activation barrier is overcome.
Surface diffusion coefficient and surface-energy anisotropy are the structural mediators controlling the evolution.
The relevant mass-transport rate scales inversely with particle radius as 1/r^3.
Surface-mediated transport overwhelms the barrier associated with sluggish bulk diffusion in ultrasmall particles.
High configurational entropy thermodynamically stabilizes a solid solution.
The lower activation energy of surface diffusion allows transport to bypass sluggish bulk diffusion in Au-Co-Cu-Ni-Pt nanoparticles.
The smallest particles have the highest chemical potential and therefore dissolve preferentially.
Surface-energy minimization drives particle-shape evolution.
The number density of particles smaller than 5 nm will decrease rapidly within the first 100 hours at 800-1000 K.
Annealing will shift the average particle-size distribution toward larger sizes.
Annealing will change the particles from faceted to spherical shapes.
The bulk composition of the surviving particles will remain equiatomic despite coarsening.
The baseline high-entropy-alloy model predicts no significant grain growth or phase separation up to 1000 K because of sluggish diffusion and mixing entropy.
Particles larger than 20 nm should be thermally stable and show minimal coarsening because bulk sluggish diffusion dominates.
The crossover temperature may depend on differing surface-segregation tendencies of Au and Pt versus Co and Ni.
Trace oxygen or residual gas can alter surface-diffusion kinetics.
